The results open new avenues for exploring geometric analysis, integrable systems, and mathematical physics through the lens of nonholonomic Ricci flows. Nevertheless, allgeometric constructions can be equivalently re-defined for the Levi Civitaconnections and holonomic frames on (semi) Riemannian manifolds.

More than two dozen short-period Jupiter-mass gas giant planets have beendiscovered around nearby solar-type stars in recent years, several of whichundergo transits, making them ideal for the detection and characterization oftheir atmospheres. We find that higher opacity atmospheres exhibit stronger day-night temperature contrasts due to reduced radiative cooling efficiency on the night side. Overall, our study highlights the fundamental role of atmospheric opacity in shaping the climate and observables of short-period gas giants. In the first paper of this series, we considersynchronously-spinning gas giants. We investigate the atmospheric dynamics of short-period extrasolar gas giant planets, focusing on how night-side temperatures are influenced by atmospheric opacity. Based ona series of numerical simulations with varying opacities, we show that thenight-side temperature is a strong indicator of the opacity of the planetaryatmosphere. Planetary atmospheres that maintain large, interstellar opacitieswill exhibit large day-night temperature differences, while planets withreduced atmospheric opacities due to extensive grain growth and sedimentationwill exhibit much more uniform temperatures throughout their photosphere's. Inaddition to numerical results, we present a four-zone analytic approximation toexplain this dependence.

Using a widely used stellar population synthesis model, we study the abilityof using pairs of AB system colours to break the well-known stellarage--metallicity degeneracy and give constraints on the two stellar-populationparameters (age and metallicity). The methodology is validated through application to observational data from nearby galaxies and star clusters. Our results suggest that a few pairs of colours can beused to constrain the two above stellar-population parameters. This will bevery useful for exploring the stellar populations of distant galaxies. This study explores the effectiveness of specific colour pairs in constraining the age and metallicity of stellar populations. This work provides a practical framework for future observational campaigns aiming to characterize stellar populations efficiently. Some other colour pairs, such as [(R-K), (u-R)], [(I-K), (u-R)],[(R-K), (u-r)] and [(i-J), (u-R)], can possibly be used for constraining thetwo parameters, too. Our analysis identifies optimal colour pairs that minimize degeneracies and enhance parameter determination accuracy. The results also showthat the stellar ages and metallicities of galaxies observed by the SloanDigital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Two-Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS) can beestimated via photometry data. It is also shown that the colours can be used inconjunction with line indices to measure stellar-population parameters.

We present a comprehensive study of the resummed cross section for jet production at hadron colliders, focusing on the inclusion of higher-order perturbative corrections within the framework of soft-collinear effective theory. The corrections weaddress arise near the threshold for the partonic reaction, when the incomingpartons have just enough energy to produce the high-transverse-momentum finalstate. The structure of the resulting logarithmic corrections is known todepend crucially on the treatment of the invariant mass of the produced jet atthreshold. Numerical evaluations are performed for proton-proton collisions at LHC energies, demonstrating improved agreement with experimental data compared to traditional fixed-order computations. Matching our resultsto available semi-analytical next-to-leading-order calculations, we deriveresummed results valid to next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy. We presentnumerical results for the resummation effects at Tevatron and RHIC energies.

This study advances the practical applicability of OF-DFT for complex materials modeling and paves the way for large-scale simulations in condensed matter physics and materials science. Orbital free methods attempt tocalculate this directly from the electron density by approximating theuniversal but unknown kinetic energy density functional. However simple localapproximations are inaccurate and it has proved very difficult to devisegenerally accurate nonlocal approximations. We focus instead on the kineticpotential, the functional derivative of the kinetic energy DF, which appears inthe Euler equation for the electron density. We introduce novel formulations of kinetic potentials that incorporate nonlocal density dependencies, which better capture quantum mechanical effects compared to conventional local approximations. We propose twononlocal orbital free kinetic potentials that reduce to known exact forms forboth slowly varying and rapidly varying perturbations and also reproduce exactresults for the linear response of the density of the homogeneous system tosmall perturbations. Orbital-Free Density Functional Theory (OF-DFT) presents a promising framework for large-scale electronic structure calculations by eliminating the need for orbitals, thereby significantly reducing computational cost. The use of these localpseudopotentials further minimizes the possible errors from the kineticpotentials. Our theory yields results for the total energies and ionizationenergies of atoms, and for the shell structure in the atomic radial densityprofiles that are in very good agreement with calculations using the fullKohn-Sham theory.

We will consider a SUSY-SU(5) with one right-handed neutrino with a large toplike Yukawa coupling. Assuming universal soft masses at high scale we computethe low-energy spectrum and subsequently the neutralino LSP relic densitytaking also into consideration SU(5) as well as the see-saw running effectsabove the gauge coupling unification scale. We found that there exists noviable region in parameter space for $\tan\beta \ler ~35$. The $\tilde{\tau}$coannihilation process starts becoming efficient for $\tan\beta \ger 35-40$.However, this process is significantly constrained by the limited range inwhich the stau is lighter than the neutralino. By embedding the minimal supersymmetric standard model within a SUSY-GUT framework, we analyze how the extended gauge structure and unified boundary conditions influence the neutralino mass spectrum and composition. The A-pole funnel region appears at very large$\tan\beta \simeq 45-50$, while the focus-point region does not make anappearance till large ($m_0,M_{1/2}$), namely a few TeV. Our results demonstrate that the interplay between SUSY-GUT boundary conditions and the seesaw-induced effects can significantly narrow the viable regions compatible with cosmological dark matter abundance.

The space velocity of a stellar black hole encodes the history of itsformation and evolution. Here we measure the 3-dimensional motion of themicroquasar GRS 1915+105, using a decade of astrometry with the NRAO Very LongBaseline Array, together with the published radial velocity. The velocity inthe Galactic Plane deviates from circular rotation by 53-80 +_ 8 km/s, wherethe range covers any specific distance from 6-12 kpc. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the kinematic properties of the black hole X-ray binary GRS 1915+105. The peculiar velocity is minimized ata distance 9-10 kpc, and is then nearly in the radial direction towards theGalactic Center. We discuss mechanisms for the origin of the peculiar velocity,and conclude that it is most likely a consequence of Galactic velocitydiffusion on this old binary, rather than the result of a supernova kick duringthe formation of the 14 Mo black hole. Utilizing multi-epoch observations from radio and infrared telescopes, we trace the motion of the system and its associated jets over an extended period.

These findings position J1128+5925 as a promising candidate for annual modulation studies, contributing to the understanding of the interstellar medium and the fine-scale structure of AGN jets. Using multi-frequency radio observations spanning over several years, we analyze the source's flux density fluctuations to identify periodic behavior. Datafor the recently discovered and highly variable IDV source J1128+5925 arepresented. We study the frequency and time dependence of the IDV in thiscompact quasar. We measure the characteristic variability time-scale of the IDVthroughout the year, and analyze whether the observed changes in thevariability time-scale are consistent with annual modulation. We discuss the implications of our results for models of interstellar scattering and the potential for using such sources to probe the Galactic interstellar medium. This study investigates the IDV source J1128+5925 as a potential candidate for exhibiting annual modulation in its variability pattern. The observed pronounced changes ofthe variability time-scale of J1128+5925 are modelled with an anisotropicannual modulation model. The observed frequency dependence of the variation isin good agreement with the prediction from interstellar scintillation. Adoptinga simple model for the annual modulation model and using also the frequencydependence of the IDV, we derive a lower limit to the distance of thescattering screen and an upper limit to the scintillating source size. Thelatter is found to be consistent with the measured core size from VLBI.

These findings contribute to understanding the early stages of planetary system development around intermediate-mass stars. Scatteredlight is detected up to 14'' from the star. The data reveal a complex, asymmetric disk structure extending from approximately 20 to 200 astronomical units (AU) from the star. The well-known ``spiral arms'' are clearly observed and theytrail the rotating disk material. Weaker arms never before reported are alsoseen. Our results provide constraints on the disk's dust mass, grain size distribution, and potential planetary influences. We identify distinct features, including a prominent inner cavity suggestive of ongoing planet formation processes. To explainthese colors, we explore the role of asymmetric scattering, reddening, andlarge minimum sizes on ISM-like grains. Radiative transfer modeling supports a flared disk geometry with a scale height increasing with radial distance. The disk colors are similar to those derivedfor Kuiper Belt objects, suggesting that the same processes responsible fortheir colors may be at work here. We argue that we are observing only thegeometrically thick, optically thin envelope of the disk, while the opticallythick disk responsible for the far-IR emission is undetected. The observedspiral arms are then structures on this envelope. The colors indicate that theextended nebulosity is not a remnant of the infalling envelope but reprocesseddisk material.

We present an examination of the kinematics and stellar populations of asample of 3 Brightest Group Galaxies (BGGs) and 3 Brightest Cluster Galaxies(BCGs) in X-ray groups and clusters. We present a comprehensive study of the spatially resolved kinematics and stellar populations of brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) and brightest group galaxies (BGGs) to investigate their formation and evolutionary histories. We findthat the BGGs and BCGs have very uniform masses, central ages and centralmetallicities. These findings support a scenario in which BCGs and BGGs grow through a combination of in-situ star formation and accretion of smaller satellites. The range of metallicity gradients observed is surprisinggiven the homogeneous environment these galaxies probe and their uniformcentral stellar populations. However, our results are inconsistent with anysingle model of galaxy formation and emphasize the need for more theoreticalunderstanding of both the origins of metallicity gradients and galaxy formationitself. We postulate two possible physical causes for the different formationmechanisms.

We report the detection of periodic (p = 1.96 hours) bursts of extremelybright, 100% circularly polarized, coherent radio emission from the M9 dwarfTVLM 513-46546. Simultaneous photometric monitoring observations haveestablished this periodicity to be the rotation period of the dwarf. Our findings suggest the presence of stable, large-scale magnetic fields capable of accelerating electrons in the magnetosphere of the ultracool dwarf. Compact sources located at the magneticpolar regions produce highly beamed emission generated by the electroncyclotron maser instability, the same mechanism known to generate planetarycoherent radio emission in our solar system. The narrow beams of radiation passour line of sight as the dwarf rotates, producing the associated periodicbursts. These results have significant implications for understanding magnetic dynamo processes and magnetospheric physics in ultracool dwarfs.

In a 2002 paper, the authors and Bruner used the new spectrum tmf to obtainsome new nonimmersions of real projective spaces. In this note, wecomplete/correct two oversights in that paper. Building on previous work that established novel nonimmersion results using tmf, we refine and extend these techniques to a broader range of dimensions. Here wegive a simple proof of those overlooked results. Secondly, we fill in a gap in the proof of the 2002 paper. There it wasclaimed that an axial map f must satisfy f^*(X)=X_1+X_2. This paper revisits the problem of nonimmersions of real projective spaces \( \mathbb{RP}^n \) through the lens of topological modular forms (tmf). However, here we show that it is true up multiplicationby a unit in the appropriate ring, and so we retrieve all the nonimmersionresults claimed in the original paper. We also identify subtle patterns in the tmf-cohomology of projective spaces that provide stronger nonimmersion criteria than classical methods.

This is a sequel of our paper hep-th/0606125 in which we have studied the{\cal N}=1 SU(N) SYM theory obtained as a marginal deformation of the {\calN}=4 theory, with a complex deformation parameter \beta and in the planarlimit. There we have addressed the issue of conformal invariance imposing thetheory to be finite and we have found that finiteness requires reality of thedeformation parameter \beta. In this paper we relax the finiteness request andlook for a theory that in the planar limit has vanishing beta functions. Our study reveals that while real beta-deformations preserve integrability and conformal invariance in the planar limit, complex beta-deformations generally break these features, leading to richer but less symmetric models. Therefore, while thefiniteness condition leads to a scheme independent result, so that theconformal invariant theory with a real deformation is physically well defined,the condition of vanishing beta function leads to a result which is schemedependent and therefore of unclear significance. We employ perturbative techniques and holographic dualities to characterize the spectrum of anomalous dimensions and correlation functions under both types of deformations.

We analyzed the timing properties using power spectral density techniques and confirmed the significance of the signal at greater than 6σ confidence level. The centroid frequency and quality factor of the QPO are consistent with models associating kHz QPOs with orbital motion at the inner accretion disk boundary. Thekilohertz QPO was only detected when the source was in a soft high-flux statereminiscent of the lower banana branch in atoll sources. Only one kilohertz QPOpeak is detected at a relatively high frequency of 1258+-2 Hz and at a singletrial significance of more than 7 sigma. Kilohertz QPOs with a higher frequencyhave only been found on two occasions in 4U 0614+09. We report the detection of a high-frequency kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillation (kHz QPO) at 1258 Hz in the ultra-compact X-ray binary 1A 1246-588. The full-width at half maximum is 25+-4 Hz, making the coherence thehighest found for an upper kilohertz QPO. From a distance estimate of ~6 kpcfrom a radius expansion burst we derive that 1A 1246-588 is at a persistentflux of ~0.2-0.3 per cent of the Eddington flux, hence 1A 1246-588 is one ofthe weakest LMXBs for which a kilohertz QPO has been detected. Theroot-mean-square (rms) amplitude in the 5-60 keV band is 27+-3 per cent, thisis the highest for any kilohertz QPO source so far, in line with the generalanti-correlation between source luminosity and rms amplitude of the kilohertzQPO peak identified before. Using the X-ray spectral information we produce acolour-colour diagram. The frequency of 1258 Hz represents the highest single kHz QPO frequency detected to date in an ultra-compact system.

Leveraging the unique nonlinear optical properties of organic materials, the proposed switch achieves rapid modulation with minimal insertion loss. In analysis section, weproposed a quantum photonic model (QPM) to explain linear electro-optic (EO)effect. This model interpret this effect by photon-electron interaction inattosecond regime. We simulate applied electric field on molecule and crystalby Monte-Carlo method in time domain. We show how a waveguide response to anoptical signal with different wavelengths when a transverse electric fieldapplied to the waveguide. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis and design methodology for an organic high-speed digital electro-optic switch. Finite element simulations validate the optical and electrical performance, demonstrating switching times on the order of nanoseconds. This switch is smaller atleast to one-half of similar DOS in dimensions.

This work establishes a robust theoretical foundation for exploring rotating quantum fluids and contributes to the understanding of superfluid dynamics in ultracold atomic systems. This method is a variationalmethod extended from the Hartree-Fock theory, which can treat the pairingcorrelations in a self-consistent manner. An advantage of this method is that afinite-range interaction between constituent particles can be used in thecalculation, unlike the original Gross-Pitaevskii approach. To demonstrate thevalidity of our method, we present a calculation for a toy model, that is, arotating system of ten bosonic particles interacting through the repulsivequadrupole-quadrupole interaction in a harmonic trap. Our calculations reveal detailed insights into the energy spectra, vortex configurations, and pairing correlations as functions of rotation frequency and interaction strength. One of such cases is a vortex state, which appears when the totalangular momentum $L$ is twice the particle number $N$ (i.e., $L=2N$).

A k-query Locally Decodable Code (LDC) encodes an n-bit message x as an N-bitcodeword C(x), such that one can probabilistically recover any bit x_i of themessage by querying only k bits of the codeword C(x), even after some constantfraction of codeword bits has been corrupted. This paper explores the construction of locally decodable codes (LDCs) derived from specially structured subsets of finite fields, termed “nice subsets.” We introduce a novel framework that leverages algebraic properties of these subsets to improve the efficiency of LDCs in terms of query complexity and code length. Recently [Y] introduced a novel technique for constructing locally decodablecodes and vastly improved the upper bounds for code length. The technique isbased on Mersenne primes. A key aspect of our approach involves the interplay between the combinatorial features of these subsets and the arithmetic of prime factors of Mersenne numbers. Specifically, we show that every Mersenne number m=2^t-1 that has a primefactor p>m^\gamma yields a family of k(\gamma)-query locally decodable codes oflength Exp(n^{1/t}). Conversely, if for some fixed k and all \epsilon > 0 onecan use the technique of [Y] to obtain a family of k-query LDCs of lengthExp(n^\epsilon); then infinitely many Mersenne numbers have prime factors argerthan known currently.

We conducted a mixed-methods approach, combining surveys and in-depth interviews, to identify common practices and challenges faced by users. We use responses to a survey of people who haverecovered lost websites, in combination with supplementary interviews, to painta fuller picture of current curatorial strategies and practices. We examine thetypes of personal, topical, and commercial websites that respondents have lostand the reasons they have lost this potentially valuable material. Based on these insights, we propose recommendations for enhancing personal archiving techniques, emphasizing the need for user-friendly tools that balance accessibility, security, and sustainability. We found that curation of personal digital materials inonline stores bears some striking similarities to the curation of similarmaterials stored locally in that study participants continue to archivepersonal assets by relying on a combination of benign neglect, sporadicbackups, and unsystematic file replication. However, we have also identifiedissues specific to Internet-based material: how risk is spread by distributingthe files among multiple servers and services; the circular reasoningparticipants use when they discuss the safety of their digital assets; and thetypes of online material that are particularly vulnerable to loss. The studyreveals ways in which expectations of permanence and notification are violatedand situations in which benign neglect has far greater consequences for thelong-term fate of important digital assets.

Vortices are pervasive in nature, representing the breakdown of laminar fluidflow and hence playing a key role in turbulence. The fluid rotation associatedwith a vortex can be parameterized by the circulation $\Gamma=\oint {\rm d}{\bfr}\cdot{\bf v}({\bf r})$ about the vortex, where ${\bf v}({\bf r})$ is thefluid velocity field. While classical vortices can take any value ofcirculation, superfluids are irrotational, and any rotation or angular momentumis constrained to occur through vortices with quantized circulation. The role of external trapping potentials and rotation frequencies in nucleating vortices is examined in detail. The recentobservation of quantized vortices in a fermionic gas was taken as a clearsignature of the underlying condensation and superfluidity of fermion pairs. We analyze the formation, stability, and dynamics of quantized vortices within the mean-field framework provided by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation.

Traditionally, it is understood that fluctuations in the equilibriumdistribution are not evident in thermodynamic systems of large $N$ (the numberof particles in the system) \cite{Huang1}. In this paper we examine thevalidity of this perception by investigating whether such fluctuations can inreality depend on temperature. The results provide a deeper understanding of the microscopic origins of macroscopic stability and the limits of deterministic thermodynamic descriptions. Furthermore, the study explores the conditions under which fluctuations may induce observable deviations from equilibrium predictions. We show that, for every system of fixed and finite $N$,fluctuations about the equilibrium distribution do, in fact, depend on thetemperature. This paper investigates the equilibrium fluctuations exhibited by an isolated thermodynamic system, emphasizing the statistical underpinnings of macroscopic stability. We term this state, where not one macrostatebut a region of macrostates closely fit the underlying distribution, a ``{\itfluctuating equilibrium}''. Finally, we speculate on how this finding isapplicable to networks, financial markets, and other thermodynamic-likesystems.

We derive modified Friedmann equations consistent with brane-world scenarios and examine their implications for early universe evolution. Our results demonstrate that the presence of additional fields can significantly enhance the inflationary phase, alleviating some limitations of single-field models. Using the scalarspectral index and the amplitude of scalar perturbations we determine both themass of the scalar fields responsible for inflation and the fundamental Planckmass of the higher-dimensional theory. We find that the mass of the scalars hasthe typical value of the inflaton mass in chaotic inflation ($M_I \sim 10^{13}$GeV) and that the five-dimensional Planck mass is very close to the GUT (GrandUnified Theories) scale ($M_5 \sim (10^{16}-10^{17})$ GeV). Furthermore, nomatter how many scalar fields we use it is not possible to have chaoticinflation with field values below the fundamental Planck mass.

Our findings provide new insights into the interplay between quantum effects and higher-dimensional compactifications in string-inspired models. The resulting Casimir force exhibits a nontrivial dependence on the warping parameters and flux quantization, revealing novel stabilization mechanisms absent in unwarped scenarios. This work opens avenues for addressing the hierarchy problem and the cosmological constant puzzle through quantum stabilization in extra-dimensional theories. The one-loop effective potential for the volume modulus has aform which is very similar to Coleman-Weinberg potential. We evaluatecoefficients appearing in the effective potential by employing zeta functionregularization and heat kernel analysis. The volume modulus is stabilized forsmaller degrees of warping, below a critical value, which depends on deficitangle of the reference brane. After stabilizing the modulus, it is possible toobtain observed values of the mass ratio between the fundamental energy scalesand a tiny effective cosmological constant (though its sign is negative). Thedegree of warping should be tuned to be close to the critical value, not asseverely as the original fine-tuning.

We present measurements of the mean dense core lifetimes in numericalsimulations of magnetically supercritical, turbulent, isothermal molecularclouds, in order to compare with observational determinations. "Prestellar"lifetimes (given as a function of the mean density within the cores, which inturn is determined by the density threshold n_thr used to define them) areconsistent with observationally reported values, ranging from a few to severalfree-fall times. We also present estimates of the fraction of cores in the"prestellar", "stellar'', and "failed" (those cores that redisperse back intothe environment) stages as a function of n_thr. We identify dense cores using a density threshold criterion and track their evolution to measure lifetimes from formation to collapse or dispersal. The results reveal a broad distribution of core lifetimes, with a significant fraction exhibiting lifetimes comparable to or shorter than their free-fall times. Our study employs high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic simulations that incorporate self-gravity, turbulence driving, and realistic initial conditions representative of star-forming regions. We also find thatthe mass in the failed cores is comparable to that in stellar cores at n_thr =1.5 x 10^4 cm^-3, but becomes negligible at n_thr = 1.2 x 10^5 cm^-3, inagreement with recent observational suggestions that at the latter densitiesthe cores are in general gravitationally dominated. We conclude by noting thatthe timescale for core contraction and collapse is virtually the same in thesubcritical, ambipolar diffusion-mediated model of star formation, in the modelof star formation in turbulent supercritical clouds, and in a modelintermediate between the previous two, for currently accepted values of theclouds' magnetic criticality.

We present the results of spectroscopy of Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs) at z~5in the J0053+1234 field with the Faint Object Camera and Spectrograph on theSubaru telescope. Our sample comprises a statistically significant number of LBGs selected via the dropout technique in deep imaging surveys, enabling robust characterization of their spectral properties. The EWs of Ly alpha emission of the 2 LBGsare not so strong to be detected as Ly alpha emitters, and one of them showsstrong low-ionized interstellar (LIS) metal absorption lines. Two faint objectswith z' \geq 25.0 mag are also confirmed to be at z~5, and their spectra showstrong Ly alpha emission in contrast to the bright ones. These results suggesta deficiency of strong Ly alpha emission in bright LBGs at z~5, which has beendiscussed in our previous paper. These insights contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of galaxy formation and evolution during the first billion years after the Big Bang. We investigate the continuum slopes, interstellar absorption lines, and Lyman-alpha emission features to probe the physical conditions of the interstellar medium and the star formation activity in these early galaxies. For a part of our sample in the HDF-N region, we obtainednear-to-mid infrared data, which constraint stellar masses of these objects.With the stellar mass and the metallicity estimated from LIS absorptions, themetallicities of the LBGs at z~5 tend to be lower than those of the galaxieswith the same stellar mass at z \lesssim 2, although the uncertainty is verylarge.

We derive the exact solution for the optical conductivity $\sigma(\omega)$ ofone hole in the Holstein-t-J model in the framework of dynamical mean-fieldtheory (DMFT). We investigate the magnetic and phonon features associated withpolaron formation as a function of the exchange coupling $J$, of theelectron-phonon interaction $\lambda$ and of the temperature. Our solutiondirectly relates the features of the optical conductivity to the excitations inthe single-particle spectral function, revealing two distinct mechanisms ofclosing and filling of the optical pseudogap that take place upon varying themicroscopic parameters. Using advanced numerical techniques, we analyze the spectral weight redistribution and the formation of mid-infrared absorption bands characteristic of polaron dynamics. These findings provide new insights into the complex charge dynamics in correlated electron systems and offer a framework for interpreting optical experiments in strongly correlated materials.

We here report on the multiwavelength study which led us to theidentification of X-ray source IGR J16194-2810 as a new Symbiotic X-ray Binary(SyXB), that is, a rare type of Low Mass X-ray Binary (LMXB) composed of aM-type giant and a compact object. Using the accurate X-ray position allowed bySwift/XRT data, we pinpointed the optical counterpart, a M2 III star. Besides,the combined use of the spectral information afforded by XRT and INTEGRAL/IBISshows that the 0.5-200 keV spectrum of this source can be described with anabsorbed Comptonization model, usually found in LMXBs and, in particular, inSyXBs. No long-term (days to months) periodicities are detected in the IBISdata. The time coverage afforded by XRT reveals shot-noise variability typicalof accreting Galactic X-ray sources, but is not good enough to explore thepresence of X-ray short-term (seconds to hours) oscillations in detail. Our findings expand the known diversity of symbiotic binaries and provide insights into their accretion mechanisms and evolutionary pathways. The X-ray emission displays persistent, soft spectra with a luminosity on the order of 10^33 erg s^-1, consistent with accretion onto a compact object.

By employing a combination of analytical modeling and numerical simulations, we examine the behavior of entropy generation across various non-linear regimes. Two important hypotheseswill be studied: the maximum entropy production (MaxEP) principle that claimsthat the selected steady state has the highest EP, and the gradient responseprinciple that claims that the EP of the selected steady state (maximally)increases when the external thermodynamic driving force increases. We willformulate these hypotheses more rigorously and present a simple chemicalreaction model to test these hypotheses. With the help of this model, we willclearly demonstrate that there are different MaxEP hypotheses being discussedin the literature and we will look at some parts in the literature where thesedifferences are not always clarified. This work lays the groundwork for refining theoretical frameworks related to entropy production in far-from-equilibrium phenomena.

Future observational campaigns and refined models are necessary to validate these theoretical predictions. One of the typical features shown by observations of solarprominence oscillations is that they are damped in time and that the values ofthe damping times are usually between one and three times the correspondingoscillatory period. The results reveal that the presence of a strong longitudinal magnetic field significantly enhances the damping rate of prominence oscillations. Aims. Thermal conduction, optically thin or thickradiation and heating are taken into account in the energy equation, and theirrole on the attenuation of prominence oscillations is evaluated. Methods. The findings suggest that the corona acts as a damping medium, facilitating the rapid attenuation of small-amplitude waves observed in prominence structures. Furthermore, our analysis underscores the importance of magnetic field orientation and plasma parameters in governing wave behavior. Our simulations incorporate realistic plasma parameters to evaluate the role of magnetic tension and thermal conduction in wave attenuation. This study investigates the influence of the solar corona on the attenuation of small-amplitude prominence oscillations, focusing specifically on the effects of longitudinal magnetic fields. Using advanced magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modeling, we analyze how coronal conditions modulate wave damping mechanisms within solar prominences. In the observed range of wavelengths theinternal slow mode is attenuated by radiation from the prominence plasma, thefast mode by the combination of prominence radiation and coronal conduction andthe external slow mode by coronal conduction. Additionally, the study demonstrates that variations in magnetic field strength influence the oscillation period and decay time, providing insights into prominence stability. Conclusions.Non-adiabatic effects are efficient damping mechanisms for magnetoacousticmodes, and the values of the obtained damping times are compatible with thoseobserved.

Applications to the theory of nilpotent Leibniz algebras and their automorphism groups are discussed. Actually, the observations show there aretwo resources to get classification of filiform Leibniz algebras. By employing cohomological methods and deformation theory, we identify new invariants that distinguish non-isomorphic algebras within this class. The classification results are presented in terms of parameterized families, highlighting the complexity and richness of the variety of filiform Leibniz algebras. Building upon the foundational results established in Part 1, we provide a comprehensive analysis of filiform Leibniz algebras of dimensions greater than five. This work lays the groundwork for future studies on the representation theory and homological aspects of filiform Leibniz algebras. Our main effort in this paper is the algebraic classification. Wesuggest here an algebraic method based on invariants. Utilizing this method forany given low dimensional case all filiform Leibniz algebras can be classified.Moreover, the results can be used for geometric classification of orbits ofsuch algebras.

A scheme for coherent manipulation of collective atomic states is developedsuch that total subradiant states, in which spontaneous emission is suppressedinto all directions due to destructive interference between neighbor atoms, canbe created in an extended atomic ensemble. By exploiting the collective interference effects inherent in subradiant states, our method suppresses spontaneous emission and mitigates decoherence mechanisms. It isshown that in order to achieve the maximum signal-to-noise ratio the shape of alight pulse to be stored and reconstructed using a homogeneously broadenedabsorbtion line of an atomic system should be a time-reversed regular part ofthe response function of the system. We develop a theoretical framework describing the preparation, manipulation, and retrieval of quantum information encoded in these states.

Our experimental design incorporates high-efficiency detectors and space-like separation to rigorously exclude local realist explanations. This study presents an experimental investigation into the validity of non-local realism, a theoretical framework proposing that physical properties are defined independently of measurement yet can exhibit non-local correlations. These findings challenge the plausibility of non-local realistic theories as a complete description of quantum phenomena. Experimentswith entangled pairs of particles have amply confirmed these quantumpredictions, thus rendering local realistic theories untenable. Maintainingrealism as a fundamental concept would therefore necessitate the introductionof 'spooky' actions that defy locality. This work contributes to the ongoing discourse on the interpretation of quantum mechanics and the limits of hidden variable theories. Our result suggests thatgiving up the concept of locality is not sufficient to be consistent withquantum experiments, unless certain intuitive features of realism areabandoned.

The derived redshift distribution reveals a preference for moderate to high redshifts, suggesting that EHBLs are more distant and possibly more luminous than previously thought. Our observations were conducted using multiple ground-based telescopes equipped with medium- to high-resolution spectrographs, enabling precise redshift measurements and spectral classification. We carried out asystematic spectroscopic campaign for the observation of all unidentifiedobjects of the sample using the ESO 3.6m, the KPNO 4m, and the TNG opticaltelescopes. Our results contribute valuable data for future theoretical modeling and high-energy observations, reinforcing the importance of optical spectroscopy in the study of EHBLs. We discuss the implications of our findings for the understanding of jet physics and particle acceleration mechanisms in blazars. We present positional and spectroscopic information for all confirmedBL Lac objects. We successfully determined redshifts for a majority of the sample, significantly improving the completeness of the Sedentary Survey. The redshiftdistribution of the complete sample is presented and compared with that ofother BL Lacs samples. The spectral features observed confirm the extreme nature of these sources, with weak or absent emission lines consistent with BL Lacertae objects. For asubsample of 38 object with high-quality spectra, we find a correlation betweenthe optical spectral slope, the 1.4 GHz radio luminosity, and the Ca H&K breakvalue, indicating that for powerful/beamed sources the optical light isdominated by the non-thermal emission from the jet.

We apply the method to a large sample of galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, demonstrating its capability to recover robust and physically meaningful histories even in the presence of observational noise. We investigate the use of an adaptative parametrization grid to recoverreliable star formation histories on a galaxy-by-galaxy basis. The results provide new insights into galaxy formation and evolution processes, emphasizing the importance of detailed spectral modeling. In this paper wedetail the method and we present our findings when we apply VESPA to syntheticand real Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) spectroscopic data. VESPA employs a flexible, non-parametric approach to decompose observed galaxy spectra into a series of simple stellar populations, enabling detailed reconstruction of star formation rates and chemical enrichment over cosmic time. We also validate the recovered histories against independent indicators such as broadband colors and emission line diagnostics, confirming the reliability of VESPA’s outputs. We find very good agreement between VESPAand our previous analysis of the SDSS sample with MOPED.

Using analytical techniques and numerical simulations, we characterize the conditions under which clusters emerge and persist in the system. Our results reveal that clustering is strongly influenced by the initial particle distribution and the stochastic rules governing particle motion. We develop a mathematical framework that captures the dynamics of particle interactions and their probabilistic behavior over time. We are interested in theasymptotic behavior of $K_n(t)$ as $n\to \infty$, where $K_n(t)$ denotes thenumber of clusters at time $t$ in the system with $n$ initial particles. Ourmain result is a functional limit theorem for $K_n(t)$. Its proof is based onthe discovered localization property of the aggregation process, which statesthat the behavior of each particle is essentially defined by the motion ofneighbor particles.

We consider the sum rule proposed by one of us (SLA), obtained by taking theexpectation value of an axial vector commutator in a state with one pion. By employing current algebra techniques alongside dispersion relations, we derive constraints on scattering amplitudes that are consistent with chiral symmetry principles. Our analysis incorporates recent experimental data to test the validity and accuracy of the sum rule predictions across various energy regimes. We alsodiscuss the related Adler--Weisberger sum rule (obtained by taking theexpectation value of the same commutator in a state with one nucleon),especially in connection with the problem of extrapolation of the pion momentumoff its mass shell. This paper presents a detailed evaluation of the axial vector commutator sum rule in the context of pion-pion scattering processes.

We analyze the properties of the quasiparticle excitations of metallicantiferromagnetic states in a strongly correlated electron system. The study isbased on dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) for the infinite dimensionalHubbard model with antiferromagnetic symmetry breaking. Self-consistentsolutions of the DMFT equations are calculated using the numericalrenormalization group (NRG). The low energy behavior in these results is thenanalyzed in terms of renormalized quasiparticles. Additionally, the effective mass enhancement and spectral function characteristics are systematically quantified, providing insights into the quasiparticle renormalization mechanisms. Comparisons with previous studies show consistency while offering new perspectives on the role of spin fluctuations in shaping the electronic structure. Our results reveal a significant restructuring of the quasiparticle band dispersion due to antiferromagnetic correlations, leading to the emergence of coherent low-energy excitations. This work advances the theoretical framework for capturing the complex behavior of quasiparticles in strongly correlated antiferromagnetic materials.

This paper proposes the response surface method for finite element modelupdating. The proposed methodology integrates RSM to construct surrogate models that approximate the relationship between model parameters and structural responses, reducing the need for extensive finite element analyses. Theupdated parameters of the finite element model were calculated using geneticalgorithm by optimizing the surface response equation. The proposed method wascompared to the existing methods that use simulated annealing or geneticalgorithm together with a full finite element model for finite element modelupdating. This framework offers a promising avenue for efficient and reliable structural model updating in engineering applications. Results indicate that the RSM-based FEMU significantly decreases computational time while maintaining high accuracy in parameter estimation. This study presents a novel approach for finite element model updating (FEMU) utilizing the response surface method (RSM) to enhance computational efficiency and accuracy.

The system's ability to adaptively distinguish between closely spaced sources underscores its practical applicability in structural health monitoring and fault diagnosis. Overall, this study contributes a novel intelligent framework that advances the state-of-the-art in AE source localization under simultaneous activation conditions. This paper presents an advanced methodology for the intelligent localization of simultaneously active acoustic emission (AE) sources, building upon the foundational concepts introduced in Part I. A difficult problem of AE analysis isseparation and characterization of signal components when the signals fromvarious sources and the mode of mixing are unknown. Furthermore, the implementation details highlight the computational efficiency achieved through optimized algorithmic design. The purpose of this paper is to demonstrate the applicabilityof ICA to locate two independent simultaneously active acoustic emissionsources on an aluminum band specimen. The method is promising fornon-destructive testing of aircraft frame structures by acoustic emissionanalysis.

We use large cosmological N-body simulations to study the subhalo populationin galaxy group sized halos. Our results reveal a universal subhalo mass function that is remarkably consistent regardless of the host halo environment, supporting the notion of self-similar substructure scaling. We examine recent claims that the earliest systems to formare deficient enough in substructure to explain the luminosity function foundin fossil groups. We investigate the substructure distributions within dark matter halos formed in a Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) cosmology to assess the existence and characteristics of fossil groups. While the number of subhalos depends weakly on the formationtime, the slope of the halo substructure velocity function does not. Utilizing high-resolution N-body simulations, we analyze the mass and spatial distributions of subhalos across a wide range of host halo masses.

We study various topological invariants on a torsional geometry in thepresence of a totally anti-symmetric torsion H under the closed condition dH =0, which appears in string theory compactification scenarios. Our approach leverages advanced techniques from differential geometry, global analysis, and non-commutative geometry to rigorously formulate and prove these extended index theorems. We extend thismodel to N=2 system, equipped with the totally anti-symmetric tensor associatedwith the torsion on the target space geometry. Next we construct transitionelements in the Lagrangian path integral formalism and apply them to theanalyses of the Witten indices in supersymmetric systems. This paper investigates index theorems within the framework of torsional geometries, extending classical results that traditionally assume torsion-free connections. We establish modified index formulas that account for the contributions of torsional components, revealing novel topological invariants associated with these geometries.

The supercritical series expansion of the survival probability for theone-dimensional contact process in heterogeneous and disordered lattices isused for the evaluation of the loci of critical points and critical exponents$\beta$. We develop a supercritical series expansion method to analyze the contact process in heterogeneous and disordered environments. We apply the method to various disorder distributions and demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing the influence of environmental heterogeneity on phase transitions. The criticalexponents in heterogeneous systems are very close to those for the homogeneouscontact process thus confirming that the contact process in periodicheterogeneous environment belongs to the directed percolation universalityclass. Our approach systematically incorporates spatial variations in infection and recovery rates, allowing for a detailed investigation of the critical behavior beyond homogeneous assumptions.

This study investigates the dynamic condensation of water at crack tips in fused silica glass, a phenomenon critical to understanding stress corrosion and crack propagation mechanisms. It is commonly understood that, duringstress-corrosion, water molecules that move in the crack cavity effectivelyreduce the bond strength at the strained crack tip and, thus, support crackpropagation. Yet the details of the environmental condition at the crack tip inmoist air are not well determined. Using high-resolution environmental scanning electron microscopy, we observed the nucleation and growth of water condensates at the crack tip under controlled humidity conditions. These results provide new insights into the microscale processes governing glass durability and failure. Wethen report new experimental data on the water condensation length increasewith relative humidity in the atmosphere. We also quantified the relationship between relative humidity, crack velocity, and condensation dynamics, highlighting the sensitivity of crack tip chemistry to environmental factors.

Furthermore, we discuss the potential signatures of such a compactification in upcoming collider experiments and gravitational wave observations. If the Casimir energy densities near one boundary result in acertain constant of integration taking a value greater than around 10^5 inunits of the d = 11 gravitational length, a form of thick pipe geometry isfound that realizes TeV-scale gravity by the ADD mechanism, with that boundarybecoming the inner surface of the thick pipe, where we live. The geometric properties of the complex hyperbolic space induce novel features in the Kaluza-Klein spectrum, which play a crucial role in lowering the fundamental gravity scale to the TeV regime. In the first alternative, the outer surface is stabilized inthe classical region and the constant of integration is fixed at around 10^{13}in units of the d = 11 gravitational length for consistency with the observedcosmological constant. By considering a compactification manifold with negative curvature, we explore the implications for the effective four-dimensional Planck scale and gauge coupling unification. Our results demonstrate that the interplay between the warped geometry and boundary gauge sectors can accommodate phenomenologically viable scenarios with large extra dimensions. Some problems related to fitting the strong/electroweak StandardModel are considered.

Our findings contribute to the broader field of disordered magnetism and have implications for designing materials with tunable magnetic properties. Using a Monte Carlo method we calculate the phase boundary T_c(x)between the ferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases. We observe a suppression of the ferromagnetic ordering temperature with decreasing x, accompanied by the emergence of glassy behavior at low concentrations. In this study, we systematically explore the phase diagram of LiHoₓY₁₋ₓF₄ across a range of Holmium concentrations (x), employing magnetization measurements, neutron scattering, and theoretical modeling. This comprehensive phase diagram advances our understanding of dilute magnetic systems and provides insight into the mechanisms governing magnetic frustration and disorder-induced phenomena. Weapply the theory of Stephen and Aharony to LiHo_{x}Y_{1-x}F_4 and find that thetheory does predict a finite-temperature freezing of the spin glass. Reasonsfor the discrepancies are discussed.

Additionally, the paper discusses potential challenges and proposes solutions to enhance the robustness of the transmission under various operational conditions. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the design strategies for the Slide-o-Cam transmission, a novel mechanism aimed at improving motion transmission efficiency and precision. Thedesign of Slide-o-Cam, a transmission intended to produce a sliding motion froma turning drive, or vice versa, was reported elsewhere. This transmissionprovides pure-rolling motion, thereby reducing the friction of rack-and-pinionsand linear drives. The results highlight the importance of precise manufacturing and assembly procedures to realize the theoretical benefits. that transmitted to the machine frame. Two alternative design strategiesare studied, namely, (i) increase the number of lobes on each cam or (ii)increase the number of cams. The study explores the fundamental principles underlying the Slide-o-Cam concept, emphasizing its potential advantages over conventional gear systems.

We study the S parameter, considering especially its sign, in models ofelectroweak symmetry breaking (EWSB) in extra dimensions, with fermionslocalized near the UV brane. Such models are conjectured to be dual to 4Dstrong dynamics triggering EWSB. This article investigates the computation of the S-parameter within the framework of holographic technicolor models, which provide a compelling approach to dynamical electroweak symmetry breaking. We explore the dependence of the S-parameter on model parameters such as the warp factor profile and the technifermion content. Additionally, we compare our holographic results with those obtained from traditional field-theoretic approaches, highlighting the advantages and limitations of each method. For the specific case of AdS_5 witha power law Higgs profile, we also show that S ~ + O(1), including effects ofpossible kinetic mixing from higher-dimensional operator (of NDA size) in the$5D$ theory. The findings provide valuable insights for the construction of viable technicolor models compatible with current experimental data.

Beginning with early observational evidence, it traces the development of theoretical models that have shaped our understanding of stellar winds and their impact on stellar lifecycles. The present state of knowledge about stellar winds, based onpapers presented at this workshop, is described. The article reviews advances in observational techniques and computational simulations that have enabled more precise quantification of mass loss rates. By integrating historical insights with recent findings, the study underscores the evolving nature of this field and its significance for broader astrophysical contexts. Attention is given to the influence of mass loss on the dynamical evolution and longevity of star clusters, including the effects on their mass functions and spatial distributions. Finally, the article outlines prospective directions for future research aimed at resolving outstanding questions in stellar and cluster evolution. The dissolution time can be derived from the mass andage distributions of cluster samples. The resulting dissolution times ofclusters in the solar neighborhood (SN) and in interacting galaxies are shorterthan predicted by two-body relaxation of clusters in a tidal field. Encounterswith giant molecular clouds can explain the fate of clusters in the SN and arethe most likely cause of the short lifetime of clusters in interactinggalaxies.

Our results reveal a pronounced modulation of the condensate density across the crystal lattice, indicating a strong spatial variation in the BEC order parameter. These findings suggest that the condensate in BaCuSi$_2$O$_6$ is not uniform but exhibits significant spatial inhomogeneity, which could influence the magnetic phase diagram. This study presents nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements to investigate the magnetic properties of BaCuSi$_2$O$_6$, a prominent quantum magnet exhibiting Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) of triplet excitations. An IC modulation of the localdensity is also present in each plane. This adds new constraints for theunderstanding of the 2D value $\phi$ = 1 of the critical exponent describingthe phase boundary.

We define angles from-to and between infinite dimensional subspaces of aHilbert space, inspired by the work of E. J. Hannan, 1961/1962 for generalcanonical correlations of stochastic processes. The spectral theory ofselfadjoint operators is used to investigate the properties of the angles,e.g., to establish connections between the angles corresponding to orthogonalcomplements. The classical gaps and angles of Dixmier and Friedrichs arecharacterized in terms of the angles. Ultimately, our contributions provide a deeper understanding of subspace interactions and their impact on numerical methods in functional analysis. The interplay between subspace geometry and operator theory is emphasized throughout the discussion, highlighting novel insights into infinite dimensional analysis. We show thatthe squared cosines of the angles from one subspace to another can beinterpreted as Ritz values in the Rayleigh-Ritz method, where the formersubspace serves as a trial subspace and the orthogonal projector of the lattersubspace serves as an operator in the Rayleigh-Ritz method. The developed theory is then applied to analyze the convergence behavior of the Rayleigh-Ritz method, a fundamental technique in numerical linear algebra and spectral approximation. Our results establish new bounds on the approximation error in terms of the principal angles between the trial subspace and the invariant subspace of the operator. Several examples illustrate the practical implications of our theoretical findings in computational eigenvalue problems.

This paper deals with the investigation of the solution of an unifiedfractional reaction-diffusion equation associated with the Caputo derivative asthe time-derivative and Riesz-Feller fractional derivative as thespace-derivative. Numerical simulations illustrate the impact of fractional orders on the spatiotemporal evolution of the system, highlighting nonlocal and history-dependent behaviors. The methodology leverages the Laplace and Fourier transform techniques to reduce the fractional partial differential equations to integral forms expressible via the H-function. By extending classical reaction-diffusion models to incorporate fractional derivatives, we capture anomalous diffusion and memory effects inherent in various complex systems. (2006a, b) for fractional reaction- diffusion equations. Finally, this study opens pathways for further research into more generalized fractional models and their analytical characterizations. These specialized types of diffusion can beinterpreted as spatial probability density functions evolving in time and areexpressible in terms of the H-functions in compact form.

We calculate the CP-violating ratio epsilon'/epsilon in the Littlest Higgsmodel with T-parity (LHT) and investigate its correlations with the branchingratios for K_L -> pi^0 nu {bar nu}, K_L -> pi^0 l^+ l^- and K^+ -> pi^+ nu {barnu}. The resulting correlations are rather strong in the case of K_L decays,but less pronounced in the case of K^+ -> pi^+ nu {bar nu}. Our analysis incorporates the latest theoretical and experimental inputs to evaluate the impact of new physics contributions on these observables. These results highlight the potential of combined measurements to probe the parameter space of the LHT model and to shed light on possible sources of CP violation beyond the Standard Model.

Devices incorporating the optimized methanofullerene nanostructures demonstrated a significant increase in power conversion efficiency compared to conventional fullerene-based solar cells. The annealing provides an enhanced mobility of the PCBMmolecules and, with good initial dispersion, allows for the formation ofexaggerated grain growth within the polymer host. This study explores the synthesis and characterization of methanofullerene elongated nanostructures to improve the performance of organic solar cells. This PCBM elongated nanostructure formationmaybe responsible for the very high efficiencies observed, at very low loadingsof PCBM (1:0.6, polymer to PCBM), in annealed photovoltaics. By controlling the nanostructure morphology, we achieved enhanced charge transport and reduced recombination losses within the active layer.

By incorporating additional vector-like matter fields and carefully analyzing their renormalization group evolution, we demonstrate that the gauge couplings converge near the Planck scale without requiring intermediate threshold corrections. Our results suggest that supersymmetry not only stabilizes the electroweak scale but also facilitates a natural embedding of the Standard Model gauge groups into a unified theory at the highest energy scales. Above the conventional GUT scale thegauge group corresponds to a left-right symmetric Supersymmetric Pati-Salammodel, which may be regarded as a ``surrogate SUSY GUT'' with all the nicefeatures of SO(10) but without proton decay or doublet-triplet splittingproblems. This study provides a compelling pathway towards a more fundamental theory that connects low-energy phenomenology with quantum gravity effects. Assuming an additional low energy $U(1)_X$ gaugegroup, identified as a non-trivial combination of diagonal $E_6$ generators,the $\mu$ problem of the MSSM can be resolved.

Near-IR and X-ray flares have been detected from the supermassive black holeSgr A* at the center of our Galaxy with a (quasi)-period of ~17-20 minutes,suggesting an emission region only a few Schwarzschild radii above the eventhorizon. Utilizing a general relativistic framework, we model the dynamics of magneto-hydrodynamic instabilities within the inner regions of the accretion disk. These results provide new insights into the complex interplay between relativistic effects and disk dynamics, offering a promising avenue to probe the immediate environment of Sagittarius A*. We find that transient disk instabilities can produce quasi-periodic oscillations with characteristic timescales consistent with recent observations of Sgr A*. We find that the Rossby wave induced spiral pattern in the disk isan excellent fit to the data, implying a disk inclination angle of ~77 deg.Note, however, that if this association is correct, the observed period is notdue to the underlying Keplerian motion but, rather, to the pattern speed. Thefavorable comparison between the observed and simulated lightcurves providesimportant additional evidence that the flares are produced in Sgr A*'s innerdisk.

We investigate the formation and subsequent collapse of quiescent cloud cores triggered by dynamic compressions within turbulent molecular clouds. Acompressive wave is set up in a constant sub-Jeans density distribution ofradius r = 1 pc. These cores exhibit properties consistent with observational data, including subsonic turbulence and centrally concentrated density profiles. Our findings provide a comprehensive framework linking turbulence, core formation, and star formation in molecular clouds. The resulting density structure resembles a quiescent core of radius <0.1 pc, with a Bonnor-Ebert-like (BE-like) profile, although it has significantdynamical differences: it is initially non-self-gravitating and confined by theram pressure of the infalling material, and consequently, growing continuouslyin mass and size. Utilizing high-resolution numerical simulations, we model the interplay between supersonic flows and self-gravity to elucidate the physical conditions leading to core formation. These results suggest thatpre-stellar cores may approximate Bonnor-Ebert structures which are however ofvariable mass and may or may not experience gravitational collapse, inqualitative agreement with the large observed frequency of cores with BE-likeprofiles.

The CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) experiment searches for axions from theSun converted into photons with energies up to around 10 keV via the inversePrimakoff effect in the high magnetic field of a superconducting Large HadronCollider (LHC) prototype magnet. Advanced shielding strategies and data analysis techniques are evaluated to mitigate background contributions. Since this signal is very rare anddifferent background components (environmental gamma radiation, cosmic rays,intrinsic radioactive impurities in the set-up, ...) entangle it, a detailedstudy of the detector background has been undertaken with the aim to understandand further reduce the background level of the detector. Our findings contribute to optimizing detector performance and bolster the scientific output of CAST in the quest to detect solar axions. The characterization of these backgrounds is essential for enhancing the sensitivity of axion searches and improving signal discrimination.

The results underscore the importance of rigorous data processing and calibration to fully exploit the capabilities of AMBER on the VLTI for astrophysical research.
